 CORE
August 22, 2025

Highlight
Show highlights
FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Explain the epidemiology of, etiology of, and risk factors for proximal radius fractures in
pediatric patients.
Perform an appropriate workup for pediatric patients in whom fracture about the elbow is
suspected.
Review the surgical and nonsurgical management of radius fractures in pediatric patients.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Most fractures are radial neck and/or physeal fractures.
Involvement of the radial head/epiphysis is uncommon; however, it occurs in Salter-Harris type
III and type IV injury patterns.




NOTES

Most are associated with extension and valgus loading of the elbow or elbow dislocation.
Epidemiology
These injuries account for approximately 14% to 20% of all injuries of the proximal radius and
affect females and males equally.1
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
The elbow follows a sequential pattern of ossification and fusion (Figure 1; Table 1).

Figure 1 Images show the ossification centers of the distal humerus. A, Illustration shows the
mean time of appearance of ossification centers at the distal humerus. B, AP radiograph of a
right elbow demonstrates the different ossification centers. 1 = capitellum, 2 = medial
epicondyle, 3 = trochlea, 4 = lateral epicondyle. (Reproduced from Gottschalk HP, Eisner E,
Hosalkar HS: Medial epicondyle fractures in the pediatric population. JAm Acad Orthop Surg
2012;20[4]:223-232.)

Osteology
On AP radiographs, a slight lateral angulation of the proximal radial metaphysis is
observed. Relative to the diaphysis, the radial metaphysis may be angulated up to 15°
valgus and 10° posterior.2 The ossific nucleus of the radius also can be bipartite, which is
a normal anatomic variation and should not be mistaken for a fracture1,3 (Figure 2).
Figure 2 Images of the elbows of young children. A, AP elbow radiograph demonstrates
normal early ossification of the distal humerus and the proximal radius. Note that the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:55 PM
AAOS | Proximal Radius Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004067
3/26

proximal radial physis is slightly wider laterally than medially. B, AP elbow radiograph
demonstrates a radial neck fracture; however, because the radial head has not yet
ossified, true displacement of the fracture is difficult to determine. C, Intraoperative AP
arthrogram of the elbow shown in panel B shows better visualization of the radial neck
fracture. The dye outlines the radial head and neck, allowing for true appreciation of the
degree of fracture displacement. (Panel A reproduced with permission from Garg S,
Erickson MA, Sibbel SE: Radial neck and olecranon fractures, in Waters PM, Skaggs DL,
Flynn JM, eds: Rockwood and Wilkins’ Fractures in Children, ed 10. Philadelphia, PA, Wolters
Kluwer, 2024, pp 336-391. Panels B and C reproduced from Nicholson LT, Skaggs DL:
Proximal radius fractures in children. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2019;27[19]:e876-e886.)
Vascular Anatomy
The blood supply to the radial head is entirely intraosseous and enters through the radial
metaphysis.
Joints and Ligaments
No direct soft-tissue attachments to the radial head or neck are present.
The annular ligament wraps circumferentially around the radial neck but arises from the radial
side of the ulna (Figure 3).
Figure 3 Illustrations of an elbow show the structure of the medial collateral ligament complex
(A) and the lateral collateral ligament complex (B). (Reproduced from Tashjian RZ, Katarincic JA:
Complex elbow instability. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2006;14[5]:278-86.)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:55 PM
AAOS | Proximal Radius Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004067
4/26


Joints and Ligaments
The annular ligament arises from the radial aspect of the ulna and wraps
circumferentially around the radial neck. This ligament also is the attachment site for the
radial (lateral) collateral ligaments. The annular ligament and lateral collateral ligaments
stabilize the radiocapitellar joints and protect against varus stress. The ulnar collateral
ligament (UCL) is composed of three bands: the anterior UCL, transverse UCL, and
posterior UCL. The ligament complex inserts on the coronoid process and the medial
olecranon. The anterior and posterior bands originate from the medial epicondyle and
resist valgus stress in elbow extension and flexion, respectively.4 The transverse
ligament runs from the olecranon to the coronoid but does not substantially contribute
to joint stability.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Falling onto an outstretched hand and sustaining a compressive force to the radiocapitellar
joint and a valgus force to the elbow applies an angular force to the neck, which may result in a
proximal radius fracture (Figure 4).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:55 PM
AAOS | Proximal Radius Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004067
5/26

Figure 4 Illustrations of an elbow show proximal radius fracture from a valgus force across the
elbow. The stout annular ligament may serve as a stress riser, predisposing the proximal radial
metaphysis to fracture. AL = annular ligament, aMCL = anterior band of the medial collateral
ligament, LUCL = lateral ulnar collateral ligament, RCL = radial collateral ligament. (Reproduced
from Nicholson LT, Skaggs DL: Proximal radius fractures in children. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
2019;27[19]:e876-e886.)
The proximal radial physis also may be at risk for chronic repetitive stress injuries, particularly
among avid youth sport athletes. The sports most commonly associated with these types of
injuries are youth baseball and gymnastics (Figure 5).
Figure 5 AP (A) and lateral (B) radiographs of the elbow of a gymnast demonstrate a proximal
radius stress fracture resulting from repetitive loading. (Courtesy of Christine Ho, MD, Dallas,
TX.)

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
The most common mechanism of proximal radius fracture is a fall onto an outstretched
hand with a concomitant valgus force across the elbow. The rotational position of the
forearm (supination, neutral, or pronation) determines the location at which the angular
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:55 PM
AAOS | Proximal Radius Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004067
6/26

force is most concentrated and, as a result, the manner in which the fracture is
angulated.1,5,6 If the forearm is in a supinated position, the forces are concentrated
anteriorly, whereas in a pronated forearm, forces are concentrated posteriorly. If a child
sustains a varus force across the elbow while falling onto an outstretched hand, he or
she may sustain a fracture of the olecranon/proximal ulna with a dislocation of the radial
head (Monteggia fracture) or a fracture through the radial neck (Monteggia fracture
variant).1 In the latter circumstance, the radial head and the proximal neck remain
aligned with the radiocapitellar joint; however, the radial metaphysis and diaphysis
displace laterally with the ulnar diaphysis.
Risk Factors
Most radial head and neck fractures in children result from acute head and neck fractures
from traumatic injury, without known predisposing risk factors.
The increase in youth athletics, year-round sports, and single-sport specialization among
children has resulted in an increasing incidence of proximal radial physis stress injuries.7
Associated Injuries
Approximately 30% to 50% of radial neck fractures are associated with other injuries, including
other fractures about the elbow and collateral ligament injuries.2
Proximal ulna fractures and olecranon fractures may occur in combination with proximal
radial neck fractures and are classified as Monteggia fracture variants.
Injury Classification
Classification is based on the location of the fracture (neck or head) and angulation and/or
displacement. Most proximal radius fractures fall into group 1 (primary displacement of the
radial head). The Judet classification of radial neck fractures is the most used classification
system.
Chambers/Jeffrey/Newman combined classification system1,6,8
Group 1: primary displacement of the radial head
A: valgus fractures
Type A: Salter-Harris type I and type II injuries of the proximal radial physisSEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:55 PM
AAOS | Proximal Radius Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004067
7/26

Type B: Salter-Harris type IV injuries of the proximal radial physis
Type C: fractures involving only the proximal radial metaphysis
B: fractures associated with elbow dislocation
Type D: reduction injuries
Type E: dislocation injuries
Group 2: primary displacement of the radial neck
Angular injuries
Torsional injuries
Group 3: stress injuries
Osteochondritis dissecans or osteochondrosis of the radial head
Physeal injuries with neck angulation
O’Brien classification system for radial neck fractures9
Type I fractures: angulated less than 30°
Type II fractures: angulated 30° to 60°
Type III fractures: angulated greater than 60°
Judet classification system for radial neck fractures2 (Figure 6)
Grade I—The proximal radial epiphysis is translated but not angulated.
Grade II—Fractures are angulated less than 30°.
Grade III—Fractures are angulated between 30° and 60°.
Grade IV
Grade IVa—Fractures are angulated 60° to 80°.
Grade IVb—Fractures are angulated 80° to 90°.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:55 PM
AAOS | Proximal Radius Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004067
8/26

Figure 6 Illustrations show the Judet classification of proximal radius fractures. (Reproduced
from Nicholson LT, Skaggs DL: Proximal radius fractures in children. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
2019;27[19]:e876-e886.)
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Most children present after an acute traumatic event, with the most common mechanism of
injury involving a fall onto an outstretched hand.

Patient History
Children with more severe injuries or who sustain fractures from a higher energy
mechanism of injury generally present for treatment immediately postinjury. Mild
injuries may initially be presumed to be a sprain, and patients and families may only
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:55 PM
AAOS | Proximal Radius Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004067
9/26

seek medical treatment if the pain does not resolve with 1 or more days of symptomatic
management. Parents of very young children may bring their child to a physician after
noticing that the child has not been using the affected extremity, preferring to lift things
and play with toys using the contralateral extremity.
Physical Examination
Isolated swelling or bruising may be observed about the proximal lateral aspect of the elbow.
In patients with a nondisplaced or minimally displaced fracture, active elbow flexion and
extension may be able to be performed with only mild discomfort; however, these patients
tend to resist supination and pronation because of pain.
The fracture location may be difficult to determine in very young children. Careful, methodic
palpation of the distal humerus, proximal ulna/olecranon, and proximal radius may help
localize the fracture location.
Neurovascular Examination
Every child should undergo a complete neurovascular examination, confirming palpable radial
and ulnar pulses and intact radial, median, and ulnar nerve sensory and motor function.
Neurovascular injury is uncommon in patients with an isolated proximal radius fracture but
can occur during traumatic fracture dislocation events.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
AP, lateral, and oblique views of the elbow are the main diagnostic radiographs necessary to
diagnose and determine management.

Radiography
Although practitioners generally are taught that the center of the radial head should be
well aligned with the center of the capitellum on all radiographic views, this line may
miss the capitellum in as many as 16% of children younger than 5 years,.10 Souder et
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:55 PM
AAOS | Proximal Radius Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004067
10/26

al11 described the lateral humeral line as a diagnostic reference line to be used to
evaluate for Monteggia fractures and proximal radial neck fractures in young children.
First, a line is drawn down the longitudinal axis of the humeral diaphysis. A second line is
then drawn parallel to the first line so that it touches the lateralmost portion of the
ossified distal humerus. This second line should fall lateral to the radial neck on an AP
view of the elbow (Figure 7). Contralateral elbow radiographs may aid in distinguishing
normal anatomic alignment of the proximal radius from traumatic malalignment,
particularly if concern exists with regard to the degree of proximal radius valgus. An
elbow arthrogram can be obtained to better evaluate the degree of fracture
displacement. This may be particularly useful in very young children in whom limited
ossification of the proximal radial epiphysis is noted (Figure 2).
Figure 7 Illustration of an elbow shows the lateral humeral line, which suggests lateral
subluxation of the radial head. (Redrawn with permission from Souder CD, Roocroft JH,
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:55 PM
AAOS | Proximal Radius Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004067
11/26

Edmonds EW: Significance of the lateral humeral line for evaluating radiocapitellar
alignment in children. J Pediatr Orthop 2017;37[3]:e150-e155.)
Computed Tomography
CT generally is not indicated because diagnosis and management often can be determined via
plain radiographs, with or without arthrograms.
CT scans may be useful for preoperative planning in older patients with a true radial head
fracture.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI typically is not necessary to diagnose and manage traumatic proximal radius fractures in
children.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
If concern for a repetitive stress injury exists, MRI may demonstrate edema and other
changes about the proximal radius physis that may confirm a proximal radius stress
injury. MRI also can help differentiate a proximal radius stress injury from other types of
repetitive stress injuries of the elbow, such as osteochondritis of the capitellum.
Differential Diagnosis
Other fractures about the elbow, including supracondylar fractures, lateral and medial condyle
fractures, and olecranon fractures—as well as Monteggia fractures and Monteggia fracture
variants—should be included in the differential diagnosis.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Most fractures are managed in a closed fashion, with or without fracture manipulation.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:55 PM
AAOS | Proximal Radius Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004067
12/26

Early mobilization minimizes stiffness.

Nonsurgical Management
Multiple closed reduction techniques have been described in the literature, and closed
reduction generally is preferred over open reduction. A high incidence of stiffness and
poor functional outcomes has been reported after open reduction; however, this may be
because of the need for open reduction in patients with more displaced and high-energy
fractures rather than because of the procedure itself. Fracture angulation greater than
60° and presentation more than 24 hours postinjury are risk factors for failed closed
reduction.12 For these injuries, splint immobilization in the emergency room followed by
outpatient surgical management may be more prudent than attempting sedated
reduction.
Indications
Fractures angulated less than 30° and with less than 3 mm of displacement can be managed
via immobilization and without manipulation.
Fractures with more than 30° angulation should be managed via attempted closed reduction.
Evaluation of forearm supination, under local or general anesthesia, should be considered to
determine if fracture alignment is acceptable. Closed reduction should be considered in
patients with limited supination and pronation. Arthrogram can be helpful to assess articular
congruity in younger children with unossified radial heads.
Contraindications
Surgical management should be considered for open fractures, particularly in the setting of a
traumatic arthrotomy so the injury site and joint can be appropriately débrided and closed.

Contraindications

9/3/26, 5:55 PM
AAOS | Proximal Radius Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004067
13/26

Aside from open fractures, no true contraindications to attempted closed reduction.
Closed reduction under general anesthesia should be considered for fractures with a
greater degree of angulation because such reduction may be difficult. If closed reduction
is unsuccessful, the surgeon can then attempt a percutaneous method of fracture
reduction under the same anesthetic event.
Techniques/Procedures
Manipulative techniques
Patterson maneuver—The elbow is held in extension and supination; distal traction is
applied, pulling the forearm into varus as direct pressure is applied to the radial head (Figure
8).
Figure 8 Illustrations of an elbow show the Patterson maneuver. Left, An assistant grabs the
arm proximally with one hand placed medially against the distal humerus. The surgeon
applies distal traction with the forearm supinated, and pulls the forearm into varus. Right,
Digital pressure applied directly over the tilted radial head completes the reduction.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:55 PM
AAOS | Proximal Radius Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004067
14/26

(Reproduced with permission from Erickson M, Garg S: Radial neck and olecranon fractures,
in Flynn JM, Skaggs DL, Waters PM, eds: Rockwood and Wilkins’ Fractures in Children, ed 8.
Philadelphia, PA, Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2015, pp 473-525.)
Israeli technique—Direct pressure is applied over the radial head with the elbow flexed 90°
as the forearm is taken from supination to pronation. Simultaneous application of a varus
force to the elbow also may aid reduction. Fluoroscopy should be used to identify the plan of
maximal fracture displacement so the surgeon can determine the location at which direct
force should be applied to maximize the likelihood of successful reduction.13
Elastic bandage—Spontaneous reduction may occur with the tight application of an elastic
bandage around the forearm and elbow.
Nonsurgical Fracture Fixation
Fixation generally is not performed if a fracture is managed nonsurgically, unless the fracture
is unstable and re-displaces during physical examination after closed reduction.
After nonsurgical management, with or without closed reduction, immobilization in a long arm
splint or cast is recommended for 2 to 3 weeks, followed by an active range of motion
program.
Outcomes
Good to excellent outcomes are reported in more than 90% of patients with a proximal radius
fracture that requires immobilization without reduction.
The rate of good to excellent outcomes declines slightly among patients who require closed
reduction and cast immobilization versus those who can be treated via immobilization alone;
reported rates range from 64% to 86%.2
Patients with greater initial displacement, patients with associated injuries, and patients
older than 10 years have an increased risk for poorer outcomes.
Closed reduction and percutaneous fracture reduction are preferred over open reduction
because elbow range of motion and function are poorer in patients who require open
reduction.
Surgical Management
Indications
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:55 PM
AAOS | Proximal Radius Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004067
15/26

Indications after attempted closed reduction
More than 30° of residual angulation
More than 3 to 4 mm of translation
Less than 45° of pronation and supination
Contraindications
Unless an absolute indication for open management exists (ie, open fracture), closed
reduction, under local or general anesthesia, should be attempted before performing
percutaneous or open reduction.
Techniques/Procedures
Percutaneous manipulation is attempted with the use of a Kirschner wire, awl, Freer elevator,
or other metallic device (Figure 9).
The wire or elevator should be inserted more distal along the lateral aspect of the forearm
than anticipated so the tip of the device is between the radial head and neck.
The device is pressed into the radial neck and used to lever the head into an anatomic
position on the neck or an improved position in relation to the neck, at which point repeat
closed reduction techniques can be used to perfect fracture alignment.
A Joker or other type of elevator also can be percutaneously inserted and used to provide a
medial to lateral directed force against the radial neck/shaft to help stabilize this fragment
during reduction of the radial head.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:55 PM
AAOS | Proximal Radius Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004067
16/26

Figure 9 AP radiographs of an elbow demonstrate percutaneous reduction of a displaced
radial neck fracture with the use of a Kirschner wire. A, Radiograph demonstrates the
displaced radial neck fracture. The Kirschner wire is inserted distal to the fracture site (B) and
used to guide the displaced fragment proximally and then medially (C). D, Radiograph
demonstrates ultimate reduction after Kirschner wire manipulation. (Reproduced from
Nicholson LT, Skaggs DL: Proximal radius fractures in children. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
2019;27[19]:e876-e886.)
In the Metaizeau technique, a flexible rod or nail is inserted retrograde from a starting point at
the distal radial metaphysis, passed across the fracture site, rotated to reduce the fracture,
and advanced into the proximal fragment (Figure 10).
A 1.4-mm to 1.8-mm wire or flexible rod with the first 1 cm of the tip of the wire/rod bent
approximately 30° is commonly used.
The tip of the rod or nail must be advanced into the proximal radial epiphysis. Axial load
across the radiocapitellar joint may prevent fracture distraction as the nail is passed.
The flexible rod or nail also can be used to stabilize the fracture after reduced
percutaneously, without the need for the rotational reduction maneuver.
Figure 10 Illustrations show percutaneous reduction of a displaced radial neck fracture via the
Metaizeau technique. A pre-bent Kirschner wire or a flexible intramedullary nail is passed from
distal to proximal through the radial styloid to the proximal epiphysis. The tip is buried in
subchondral bone, and the wire is rotated to reduce the displaced proximal fragment.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:55 PM
AAOS | Proximal Radius Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004067
17/26

(Reproduced from Nicholson LT, Skaggs DL: Proximal radius fractures in children. J Am Acad
Orthop Surg 2019;27[19]:e876-e886.)
Open reduction rarely is necessary but may be required for severely displaced fractures.
This is performed via the posterolateral approach, with the forearm in a maximally pronated
position to rotate the posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) away from the surgical site.
Internal fixation is strongly recommended after open reduction.
Internal fixation is performed only for fractures that are unstable after reduction.
Preoperative Planning
The surgeon should be familiar with multiple types of closed and percutaneous reduction
techniques to maximize the likelihood of successful reduction.
A stepwise approach is used to minimize the invasiveness of management and to limit the risk
of associated osteonecrosis and stiffness. Closed reduction with manipulation should be
attempted first. If this fails, percutaneous reduction should be attempted, with or without
fixation. If percutaneous reduction fails, open reduction should then be performed.
If the Metaizeau technique is attempted, flexible intramedullary rods or long Steinmann pins
are necessary. Other tools for percutaneous reduction, including Kirshner wires and a freer
elevator, also should be available.
Iopamidol dye for arthrography may aid in visualization of the radial head and make fracture
alignment and radiocapitellar joint alignment easier to determine before and after reduction
(Figure 11).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:55 PM
AAOS | Proximal Radius Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004067
18/26

Figure 11 Images of the elbow of a 6-year-old boy. A, AP radiograph demonstrates a radial
neck fracture; however, because the radial head has not yet ossified, true displacement of the
fracture is difficult to determine. B, Intraoperative AP arthrogram shows closed reduction and
pinning of the radial neck fracture. The dye outlines the unossified portions of the radial head,
facilitating visualization and confirmation that the radial head is well aligned with the
capitellum after reduction. (Courtesy of Christine Ho, MD, Dallas TX.)
Patient Positioning
Patients can be placed in the supine position, with the affected extremity outstretched on a
radiolucent arm board or directly on the C-arm, according to surgeon preference.
Surgical Approaches
If open reduction is indicated, a posterolateral (Kocher) approach between the anconeus and
the extensor carpi ulnaris is used to expose the proximal radius.
The forearm must be maintained in a maximally pronated position to rotate the PIN away
from the surgical field during dissection.
Surgical Fracture Fixation
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:55 PM
AAOS | Proximal Radius Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004067
19/26

Fracture fixation generally is not indicated if the fracture is stable after closed or percutaneous
reduction. Fracture stability after reduction is evaluated by pronating and supinating the
forearm under live fluoroscopy.
If the Metaizeau technique is used, the intramedullary nail or wire is left in place as internal
fixation. Otherwise, percutaneous Kirschner wire fixation can be performed to add stability to
the fracture after reduction.
In younger children who undergo open reduction and internal fixation of a radial head
fracture, Kirschner wires generally are used. Headless compression screws or a plate-and-
screw construct may be used as the fracture pattern dictates; these types of fixation are not
commonly used in skeletally immature patients.
Postoperative Management
The elbow typically is immobilized in a long arm cast or splint for 2 to 3 weeks, after which the
patient is transitioned to a range of motion program to prevent stiffness.
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Multiple studies have shown that patients in whom successful reduction is attained via a
closed or percutaneous fashion have superior range of motion and better functional outcomes
than patients who undergo open reduction.1,2 This may be related to the severity of the injury
more than the need for surgical reduction. Regardless, a thorough understanding of multiple
closed and percutaneous reduction techniques is essential to maximize the likelihood of
successful closed or percutaneous reduction.
With the percutaneous Kirschner wire or Freer reduction technique, the insertion point of the
Kirschner wire or Freer elevator is dictated by the angular deformity of the fracture. Fractures
with greater degrees of angulation require a more distal insertion point along the forearm to
be able to pass the wire or the Freer elevator into the space between the radial head and neck
to lever the head into a reduced position.
Complications
Nonunion
Nonunion is rare.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:55 PM
AAOS | Proximal Radius Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004067
20/26


Nonunion
Waters and Stewart14 reported on nine patients who sustained a proximal radius
nonunion. All the patients had undergone open reduction after failed attempted closed
reduction.14 In contrast to nonunion, radial head overgrowth occurs in 20% to 40% of
injuries; however, this does not typically result in functional impairment.5,15
Malunion
Malunion of an angulated radial neck fracture may alter radiocapitellar joint mechanics and
affect elbow range of motion and forearm rotation.
If the radial head impinges on the capitellum, it may result in repetitive injury to the capitellar
cartilage and degenerative changes and arthritis.
Proximal Radius Growth Arrest
Radial head overgrowth occurs in 20% to 40% of patients; however, it typically does not result
in functional impairment.5,15
Soft-Tissue Reaction
Myositis ossificans can occur but may not be symptomatic.
Proximal radioulnar synostosis can occur and is most commonly observed after open
reduction.
Stiffness
Elbow stiffness is the most common complication and may occur in as many as one-third of
patients.2 Multiple attempts at closed reduction and injuries requiring open reduction are
associated with the greatest risk of postoperative stiffness. Therefore, maximizing the
likelihood of successful closed reduction is important.
Fractures should be reduced as soon as possible postinjury because a delay in reduction
increases the risk for stiffness and poor functional outcomes. Delayed management also
makes successful closed or percutaneous reduction less likely.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:55 PM
AAOS | Proximal Radius Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004067
21/26

Deciding to perform closed reduction under general anesthesia for severely angulated
fractures allows the surgeon to have the patient fully relaxed during reduction attempts,
which may make difficult reductions easier.
Being familiar with multiple closed reduction and percutaneous reduction techniques and
having the necessary equipment available if percutaneous reduction is necessary increases
the likelihood of successful reduction via a closed or percutaneous fashion.
Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
Neurologic and vascular injury as a result of the management of proximal radial fractures are
uncommon.
In patients who require open reduction, surgeons must maintain the forearm in maximal
pronation to rotate the PIN anteriorly and away from the surgical field. Otherwise, injury to the
PIN is possible during this approach.
Other Complications
Osteonecrosis of the radial head, particularly as a complication of open reduction of proximal
radius fractures, has been described.1
Rehabilitation
Stiffness is the most common complication, regardless of management.
Therefore, a brief period of immobilization (1 to 3 weeks, depending on the severity of the
fracture) followed by a return to elbow range of motion is important to prevent loss of motion.
Outcomes
The reported rate of good to excellent outcomes in patients with a proximal radius fracture
vary and are correlated with numerous factors.
According to several studies, the initial severity of angulation/fracture displacement directly
correlates with the likelihood of good to excellent functional outcomes, even in fractures that
are managed in a closed or percutaneous fashion.
However, among patients who require reduction, those with near anatomic alignment after
reduction have better overall functional outcomes than those with residual displacement.16

Both Basmajian et al17 and Zimmerman et al16 reported that children older than 10 years

Outcomes
Multiple studies have shown that patients who undergo open reduction have poorer
functional outcomes and an increased likelihood of osteonecrosis, nonunion, and
proximal radioulnar synostosis than patients who are treated via closed reduction.
Because open reduction typically is reserved for severely displaced injuries that cannot
be reduced via closed means, whether these poor outcomes result from surgical
management or the severity of the initial injury is difficult to determine.
Pearls and Pitfalls
The surgeon should be familiar with various closed and percutaneous reduction techniques to
increase the likelihood of successful closed reduction in patients who require reduction.
Studies have published different recommendations on the management of fractures
angulated 30° to 45°, with some studies18 advocating closed reduction for all fractures
angulated more than 30° and other studies15 reporting that angulation as great as 45° may be
acceptable without closed reduction. For in-between fractures in which the need for closed
reduction may not be clear, local anesthetic injection into the radiocapitellar joint followed by
gentle forearm rotation should be considered to evaluate the patient’s ability to pronate and
supinate. Closed versus percutaneous fracture reduction should be considered in patients
with restricted pronation and supination less than 70°.2
Regardless of management, limited immobilization postinjury, followed by the initiation of a
range of motion protocol, may help prevent stiffness.
